name: Money Buys Less Happiness Now
description: You can never buy enough happiness, so here we go again! In this version, you can only buy $$$h_i = 1$$$ unit of happiness each month, but the number of months is hugely increased. We are in the realm of quantum happiness and time dilation. Being a physicist, Charlie likes to plan his life in simple and precise terms. For the next $$$m$$$ months, starting with no money, Charlie will work hard and earn $$$x$$$ pounds per month. For the $$$i$$$-th month $$$(1 \le i \le m)$$$, there'll be a single opportunity of paying cost $$$c_i$$$ pounds to obtain one unit of happiness. You cannot buy more than one unit each month. Borrowing is not allowed. Money earned in the $$$i$$$-th month can only be spent in a later $$$j$$$-th month ($$$j \gt i$$$). Since physicists don't code, help Charlie find the maximum reachable units of happiness.
input_specification: The first line of the input contains $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers, $$$m$$$ and $$$x$$$ ($$$1 \le m \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$1 \le x \le 10^3$$$) — the total number of months and the monthly salary. The second line of each test case contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$c_1, c_2, \dots, c_m$$$ ($$$1 \leq c_i \leq 10^3$$$) — the cost of one unit of happiness for each month. It is guaranteed that sum of $$$m$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output one integer — the maximal amount of happiness Charlie can get.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1974G — Money Buys Less Happiness Now  [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
